metadata.title: Learning representations by back-propagating errors
metadata.authors: David E. Rumelhart, Geoffrey E. Hinton, Ronald J. Williams
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Layered feed-forward network
nodes.statement: A network with a layer of input units at the bottom, any number of intermediate (hidden) layers, and a layer of output units at the top. Connections within a layer or from higher to lower layers are forbidden, but connections may skip intermediate layers.
nodes.statement_clean: A multilayer neural network where signals flow strictly from input layer through hidden layers to output layer.

nodes.name: Total input to a unit
nodes.statement: The total input $x_j$ to unit $j$ is a linear function of the outputs $y_i$ of units connected to $j$ and of the weights $w_{ji}$ on those connections: $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Each unit's net input is the weighted sum of incoming activations.

nodes.name: Logistic (sigmoid) output function
nodes.statement: A unit's real-valued output $y_j$ is a non-linear function of its total input: $y_j = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x_j}}$.
nodes.statement_clean: Each unit applies the logistic sigmoid to its net input to produce its activation.

nodes.name: Bias as extra input
nodes.statement: Units are biased by introducing an extra input that always has value $1$; the weight on this extra input is the bias and is equivalent to a threshold of opposite sign.
nodes.statement_clean: A bias term is implemented as a weight to a constant input of value 1.

nodes.name: Total error $E$
nodes.statement: For a fixed set of input-output cases, the total error is $E = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_c \sum_j (y_{j,c} - d_{j,c})^2$, where $c$ indexes input-output pairs, $j$ indexes output units, $y_{j,c}$ is the actual state and $d_{j,c}$ the desired state.
nodes.statement_clean: Sum-of-squared-errors loss between actual and desired outputs over all training cases and output units.

nodes.name: Learning internal representations in multilayer networks
nodes.statement: Find a set of weights for a layered network with hidden units such that, for each input vector, the produced output vector matches (or is sufficiently close to) the desired output vector, where the desired states of the hidden units are not specified by the task.
nodes.statement_clean: Train a multilayer net so its outputs match targets, despite having no targets for hidden units.

nodes.name: Output-error derivative
nodes.statement: For a particular case (suppressing index $c$), differentiating the error with respect to an output unit's activation gives $\partial E / \partial y_j = y_j - d_j$.

nodes.name: Chain rule through the sigmoid
nodes.statement: Applying the chain rule and differentiating $y_j = 1/(1+e^{-x_j})$ yields $\partial E / \partial x_j = \partial E / \partial y_j \cdot y_j (1 - y_j)$.

nodes.name: Weight derivative
nodes.statement: For a weight $w_{ji}$ from $i$ to $j$: $\partial E / \partial w_{ji} = \partial E / \partial x_j \cdot \partial x_j / \partial w_{ji} = \partial E / \partial x_j \cdot y_i$.

nodes.name: Back-propagated error to lower layer
nodes.statement: Summing over all connections emanating from unit $i$: $\partial E / \partial y_i = \sum_j \partial E / \partial x_j \cdot w_{ji}$.

nodes.name: Vanilla gradient descent update
nodes.statement: The simplest version of gradient descent changes each weight by an amount proportional to the accumulated error gradient: $\Delta w = -\varepsilon \, \partial E / \partial w$.

nodes.name: Momentum (acceleration) update
nodes.statement: An acceleration method modifies the velocity in weight space rather than its position: $\Delta w(t) = -\varepsilon \, \partial E / \partial w(t) + \alpha \, \Delta w(t-1)$, where $\alpha \in (0,1)$ is an exponential decay factor.

nodes.name: Back-propagation
nodes.statement: Two-pass learning procedure: a forward pass computes unit states layer by layer using $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$ and $y_j = 1/(1+e^{-x_j})$, then a backward pass propagates $\partial E / \partial y$ from output to input through equations (4)-(7) and updates weights by gradient descent.
nodes.statement_clean: Iterative supervised learning algorithm that adjusts network weights by propagating error derivatives backward through layers.
input: Set of input-output training cases $\{(\text{input}_c, d_c)\}$
output: Learned internal representations in the hidden units

nodes.name: Initialize with small random weights
nodes.statement: To break symmetry, start with small random weights (e.g. uniformly distributed in $[-0.3, 0.3]$ as in the symmetry experiment).

nodes.name: Forward pass
nodes.statement: Set the input units to the input vector. For each layer in turn (bottom to top), compute $x_j = \sum_i y_i w_{ji}$ and $y_j = 1/(1+e^{-x_j})$ for every unit $j$ in that layer.

nodes.name: Initialize output-layer error derivatives
nodes.statement: For each output unit $j$, compute $\partial E / \partial y_j = y_j - d_j$.

nodes.name: Backward propagation of error derivatives
nodes.statement: For each layer from top to bottom, compute $\partial E / \partial x_j = \partial E / \partial y_j \cdot y_j (1 - y_j)$ and propagate down via $\partial E / \partial y_i = \sum_j \partial E / \partial x_j \cdot w_{ji}$ to obtain derivatives for the layer below.

nodes.name: Compute weight gradients
nodes.statement: For every weight $w_{ji}$ compute $\partial E / \partial w_{ji} = \partial E / \partial x_j \cdot y_i$.

nodes.name: Update weights
nodes.statement: Either change weights after every case or accumulate $\partial E / \partial w$ over all cases first; then apply $\Delta w(t) = -\varepsilon \, \partial E / \partial w(t) + \alpha \, \Delta w(t-1)$.

nodes.name: Repeat over sweeps
nodes.statement: Repeat the forward and backward passes over the training set for many sweeps until error is acceptably small (e.g. 1,425 sweeps for the symmetry task; 1,500 sweeps for the family-tree task).

nodes.name: Sigmoid is not essential
nodes.statement: It is not necessary to use exactly the functions in equations (1) and (2); any input-output function with a bounded derivative will do. The linear input combination simply makes the procedure simpler.

nodes.name: Per-case vs accumulated updates
nodes.statement: One way is to change weights after every input-output case (no separate gradient memory needed); the alternative used in this paper accumulates $\partial E / \partial w$ over all cases before changing the weights.

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking by random initialization
nodes.statement: To break symmetry the procedure starts with small random weights; otherwise units in the same layer would receive identical updates.

nodes.name: Independent discovery of the procedure
nodes.statement: Variants of the learning procedure have been discovered independently by David Parker (personal communication) and by Yann Le Cun.

nodes.name: Weight decay
nodes.statement: To make hidden-unit interpretations easier, 'weight-decay' was introduced by decrementing every weight by 0.2% after each weight change; the decay was balanced by $\partial E / \partial w$, so the final magnitude of each weight indicates its usefulness in reducing the error.

nodes.name: Local minima are rarely a problem in practice
nodes.statement: Although the error surface may contain local minima, experience with many tasks shows that the network gets stuck in poor local minima only when it has just enough connections; adding extra connections opens paths around the barriers in lower-dimensional subspaces.

nodes.name: Biological implausibility
nodes.statement: The learning procedure, in its current form, is not a plausible model of learning in brains; nevertheless it suggests that searching for biologically plausible ways of doing gradient descent in neural networks is worthwhile.

nodes.name: Mirror-symmetry detection
nodes.statement: A network with one hidden layer of two units learns to detect mirror symmetry of binary input vectors of length 6 ($64$ possible patterns). With $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $\alpha = 0.9$, and weights initialized uniformly in $[-0.3, 0.3]$, the network converges in 1,425 sweeps to a solution where, for each hidden unit, weights symmetric about the input midpoint are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
nodes.statement_clean: Backprop trains a tiny net to detect 1D mirror symmetry; the discovered weights have the analyzed symmetric structure.

nodes.name: Family-trees / distributed representations
nodes.statement: A five-layer network with 24 person-input units and 12 relationship-input units learns 100 of 104 possible $\langle\text{person1, relationship, person2}\rangle$ triples from two isomorphic family trees ($\varepsilon = 0.005$, $\alpha = 0.5$ for first 20 sweeps, then $\varepsilon = 0.01$, $\alpha = 0.9$; 1,500 sweeps with weight decay $0.2\%$). Hidden units learn distributed features such as nationality, generation, and family branch.
nodes.statement_clean: Backprop on isomorphic family trees discovers distributed hidden features (nationality, generation, branch).

nodes.name: Recurrent net unrolled as layered net
nodes.statement: A synchronous iterative net run for three iterations is equivalent to a layered net with shared weights: by storing intermediate states for the forward pass and constraining corresponding weights to remain equal (averaging $\partial E / \partial w$ over all copies), back-propagation can be applied directly to iterative nets.
nodes.statement_clean: Recurrent networks can be trained by unrolling them through time and tying weights across copies.

nodes.name: Necessity of intermediate units for symmetry detection
nodes.statement: Detecting whether the binary activity levels of a one-dimensional array of input units are symmetric about the centre point cannot be done by directly connecting input units to output units; an intermediate layer is essential. (Formal proof given in ref. 2.)
nodes.statement_clean: Without hidden units, no perceptron can decide mirror-symmetry of a binary input vector.
assumptions: A single-layer perceptron connects input units directly to one output unit
Inputs are binary activity levels of a one-dimensional array
conclusions: No such single-layer network can decide whether the input is symmetric about its centre
